utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I notice the absence and I want to record the absence of the accused Borovcanin. Today, all the other accused are present. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that Mr. Borovcanin is not feeling well. He got ill yesterday, and he couldn't come to the trial for today. The waiver is on its way, and he is not objecting to -- for the proceedings to continue without his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I take your assurance on that. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. Mr. Nikolic, is Mr. Ostojic having problems? He was to be back by Monday. By today, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am expecting him to arrive in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Prosecution, appearing today is Mr. McCloskey, accompanied by Mr. Nicholls. All right. I understand there are some preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As you know, a motion was filed on Friday by the Prosecution requesting that a certain number of Beara witnesses be barred from testifying until additional information had been provided in respect of some of them, and also that disclosure of any prior statements under 67(A)(ii) be affected. Now, we rise this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Gosnell. Sorry for interrupting you like this. It's not in my style. But we haven't got a clue as to the motion or its filing, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are better informed than we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I know the Prosecution was burning the midnight oil, literally, and they distributed a courtesy copy. And I understand it's in the process of being filed, so I understand why it hasn't reached the Bench as yet. In substance, they object -- they filed a motion that they indicated orally they would be filing, and one of the grounds for their objection to a certain number of the witnesses is failure by the Beara Defence to disclose all prior statements, as they are obliged to do under Rule 67(A)(ii). Now, the reason why we're concerned with this motion and the reason why we support it in respect of two of the witnesses is that two of these witnesses do concern our client. They are very critical witnesses, potentially, and they may be able to give information that is adverse to our client. We don't know yet, because the information in the 65 ter disclosure does not appear adverse, but we have reason to believe, based upon some previous statements, that the Prosecution may exploit some of those previous statements to elicit information that might be adverse. Now, Mr. President, yesterday a proofing note was sent around from the Beara Defence, making reference to a number of statements given by Mr. Jovanovic, and during a proofing session with my colleague, Mr. Jovanovic indicated he had testified before a state court. We don't have that transcript, and it was never disclosed by the Beara Defence. We understand as well that that transcript is never disclosed to the Prosecution. Now, this is a serious deficiency and causes us very serious prejudice, in light of the fact, Mr. President, that we need to make our choice as to how and whether to cross-examine this witness, without having any idea as to what prior statements this witness has and whether they have been given to the Prosecution, and whether they're going to be used by the Prosecution, and how. So, Mr. President, that puts us in a very difficult situation. We're flying blind in a storm. We don't know what's coming up, and we ought to have that information. And so we respectfully request, as the Prosecution did, that the testimony of these witnesses be adjourned, delayed, barred, until such time as we have that information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as regards the testimony of Miladin Jovanovic, we talked to him on Saturday and yesterday afternoon, and it turned out, on that occasion, that he stated that he had testified before the BH Court. But in our conversation later on, it was ascertained that we only have his statement that he gave to the investigative organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so we don't have this statement that he allegedly gave to a BH Court. As we went on in our conversation with him, we realised that he doesn't really distinguish between various organs such as the investigative organs, the court, and the state agency for investigations, so we don't have this testimony. We don't know where he testified, before what court. The only thing we do have is the statement that he gave to the investigative organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In principle, I am not opposed to the delay of his testimony if we were in a position to actually locate those statements and disclose them, because that would be in line with the right of all the accused to the fair trial. This statement, his statement, was given -- was first envisaged to be given under Rule 92 bis, but later on when the Prosecution opposed it, he was called as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, I don't know who is taking this up. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, most of this Mr. Nicholls will be able to talk to you about. Mr. Jovanovic is my witness. This does have to do with what I said the other day. This is having a knock-on effect to the other Defence teams, and my witness is Mr. Jovanovic that's coming up. We have found the audio of the state court that we have. We're not sure whether we have provided it to anyone at this point. We normally, even though it's not our witness, we try to get this material out to the Defence, for obvious reasons, and I'm not sure we did or not. We're -- we do have an audio of this guy's state court testimony. We don't have a transcript of it. And as for any other details regarding the motion, Mr. Nicholls can refer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which proceedings did he testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This person is always talked about being at the Kravica warehouse, and as everybody is aware, there's a big Kravica trial going on in the state court, and so when we were hustling to find materials for these people, we did get an audio from the state court. I'm not sure when we got it, I'm not sure if we turned it over or not. But he's -- this is a public trial and everyone has equal access to these folks. We happened to get it, and we're not sure we gave it to the folks. I would trust my colleagues. If they'd got it, they would have known they'd got it. But we do have this audio. But as for the motion and the rest of the week, Mr. Nicholls can speak to that, or I can answer any other questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And my understanding is that Mr. Jovanovic was supposed to testify immediately after the next witness. The next witness is Pereula?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. There are solutions to this problem, in any case. I mean, we could proceed on the basis of what we have, and he will be recalled, if necessary, later on if there are facts or issues arising from undisclosed hitherto documents. All right. But let me -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for your information, Your Honours, I believe the situation is the same for the following witness, Vasovic also a witness who will talk about events at the Kravica warehouse, who also testified in the Kravica trial in the state court. Same situation, we have found that we have the audio of that testimony. We don't have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that guy's name was not brought up by Mr. Gosnell, so I would imagine that the situation is not the same. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason why I didn't actually make reference to Mr. Vasovic is that we're not sure, frankly. We don't know whether there's another statement out there or transcript out there. We have no idea. We do know that in respect of Mr. Jovanovic. And I'm pleased to hear from my friend that in fact we now know there is a transcript of his testimony. So in that sense, Mr. President, yes, the same issue does arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, a little more information for you. We did disclose the audio of Perica Vasovic, and I'm still looking for the other witness. I wouldn't be surprised if it had been routinely, that is, disclosed when it comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you disclose it; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In March of this year. The -- and, you know, and again this is just a problem and effect of the trickle of information we're getting of who's going to say what and when, and I think that's laid out in our motion. I also, when my friend Mr. Gosnell spoke, wanted to tell Your Honours that in our motion we had collectively listed our witnesses for whom we were asking relief. However, my -- our plan today was to stand up and be ready to go ahead with Vasovic and Jovanovic, based on what we've been doing and working and looking at all the information we have. We do not have transcripts of the audio, but we do have the audio of Vasovic, which was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Anyway, let's start now. We need to discuss a little bit further amongst ourselves. Let's start with Pereula's testimony, and then we'll come back to you later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Pereula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to give evidence, being summoned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as a witness by the Defence team of Colonel Beara. Before you do so, you are required to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text is being forwarded to you now by Madam Usher. Please read it aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nikolic for the Beara Defence team will go first. He will then be followed on cross-examination by others. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pereula.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We've met, but let us do this officially. Let me first introduce myself and then make a couple of introductory remarks in order to facilitate your testimony. So my name is Predrag Nikolic, and I am Defence counsel in Ljubisa Beara's Defence team. I will now ask you to make a pause before answering, because you have to bear in mind that our conversation is being interpreted and we have to give enough time for the interpreters to do their job. If you don't do that, this will result in chaos and the transcript will not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please introduce yourself to the Court, your full name, date, and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I'm Spiro Pereula. I was born on the 10th of November, 1941. My father's name is Stevo, mother's name is Bozana. I was born in Brozolica [phoen], Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me about your education, and what qualifications do you have?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I graduated from the Teachers' High School and then the Teaching Academy, the Faculty of Defence in Sarajevo. All those schools I completed in Sarajevo. And I have to note here that I served in the army in Bileca. That was the Reserve Officers' School. That was 1962 and 1963. I started in 1962, and this extended into 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now explain to me briefly your career? What kind of jobs did you have until the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Are you referring to military service or general?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I taught in the Rogatica municipality. I was a teacher, because they paid for my education, so I had to work. And then in 1963 and in 1964, I worked in Zepa, again as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula and Mr. Nikolic, please slow down. You are already going pretty fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Do I have to repeat my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I paid back my debt to the Rogatica municipality, I moved to Sarajevo, where I worked for seven years as a teacher in the Dositej Obradovic High School. On the 1st of April, 1976, I transferred to the city staff of the Territorial Defence, and then in 1977 I went to Pancevo, where I attended a course for security officers. After completing that course and after I returned to Sarajevo, I was appointed to the Territorial Defence District Staff in Sarajevo as the security officer or security organ. I remained there until 1982, when I was transferred to the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was appointed the assistant chief of security in the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence. At that time, it was Colonel Nikola Andjelic. He was the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, I was in Sarajevo. I was still at that post in the Territorial Defence Republican Staff. When the war broke out, I and all the other members of Serb, Muslim, Croat ethnicity joined their ethnic group, so I went to the Main Staff sometime in May 1992. That was in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, were you deployed in the Main Staff and what were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: When I arrived at the Main Staff in Han Pijesak, I was deployed as the desk officer for security at the Security Administration, which was part of the Intelligence and Security Section. That was the beginning, and that's when the army was formed, the army of Republika Srpska, including the security service as part of that organisation. It was primarily my job to man the units or to provide the security organs in the units, to train these security organs, and also I dealt with additional counter-intelligence tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were deployed to the Main Staff Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the administration's organisation and who was at the head?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: At the time in May, when I arrived at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, by establishment this was the sector for security and intelligence, assignments comprising two administrations, the Security Administration and the Intelligence Administration. At the head of the sector for the intelligence and security jobs was a colonel at the time, and now his rank is that of general, Zdravko Tolimir. At the same time, he headed, at this initial period, the Security Administration, while the chief of the intelligence section was Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long were you at the Security Administration of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I was there until November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And during that period, was Colonel Ljubisa Beara there at the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. Warship Captain Ljubisa Beara to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska at Han Pijesak, came there in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what were his duties at that time?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Since Beara was trained as a security person and had a lot of professional experience, he was appointed chief -- or actually at the time, I'm not exactly sure, he was the assistant of the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security department, in charge of security and intelligence, so he was actually heading the intelligence sector of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was qualified or that he was trained for this, does that mean that you knew him from before?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no. I met Colonel Beara when he came to the Main Staff, but I heard, primarily from Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, that he had been in the security organ in the JNA, in the navy at that time in Split. And since I also had a lot of experience in security assignments, in contacts and at meetings and while receiving assignments from Mr. Ljubisa Beara, I sensed that he had a lot of skill and a good sense for organising the assignments, and he issued the assignments to me in an expert and professional way. I have to emphasise here that in all of our meetings, Mr. Ljubisa Beara was always warning us, his subordinates, and drawing our attention that while we carried out our assignments, primarily counter-intelligence ones, we had to adhere to the rules of the security organs, the methods and the means of work, as well as all the regulations in the army and in international conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, I can see that you did cooperate with Ljubisa Beara. Was he your superior?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Crna Rijeka, the Security Administration there, he was my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, what was the attitude of Officer Beara, not only towards you but towards all his subordinate officers, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I already said that in meetings of the Security Administration, he had a very professional attitude, issued specific and precise assignments to us, and he had the same attitude towards the subordinate security organs, primarily his immediate subordinates at the level of the corps and then further down, lower-ranking units at the -- in relation to the security chiefs in the corps. During the period that I was in Crna Rijeka, I myself did not have any objections, nor did I hear any from anyone else, in relation to his work and the assignments that he issued to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, when you came to the Main Staff, you said that Colonel Tolimir was at the head of that sector. During the time that Colonel Beara came, was Colonel Tolimir -- just wait, please -- was Colonel Tolimir the person in charge of that sector at that time also?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. During the time that I was in Crna Rijeka, there was the Sector for Intelligence/Security Affairs, and General Tolimir was at the head of that sector, and Mr. Ljubisa Beara was at the head of the Security Administration. I have to emphasise here that before you actually asked me about my duties and assignments before Mr. Ljubisa Beara came, I was engaged on jobs to interrogate prisoners of war. I think this was in May 1992, when we had such people. So I interrogated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a problem here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I'm going to object to non-responsive. I didn't object before. The question was: "At this time, was Tolimir in charge of the sector at the time?" And the witness answered that question and is now going on to another topic. The previous question was: "Did you know Colonel Beara from before?" And the witness then went on to another topic. So no disrespect to the witness, but if we could keep it question-answer, question-answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I can't quite understand your point, but at the same time he must have remembered something additional that he wished to tell us. So I wouldn't attach too much importance to it, not to diminish your concerns. I mean, I don't mean that, but there is a difference between one case of non-responsive answers and another. Mr. Nikolic, in the meantime, Mr. Pereula, you should try to answer the questions that are put to you. In addition to that, you would like to add something, will you please tell us first so that we authorise you to go beyond what was being asked -- what's being asked of you. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, we would just kindly ask you to respond to our questions precisely and we in that way we will cover everything more quickly.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the level of the VRS, how was the security service organised, or, rather, the security organs?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I already said at the level of the Main Staff, by establishment, there was a security and intelligence sector as part of which there were two administrations, the Security and the Intelligence Administration. At the level of the corps, there were sections for security, and at the level of the brigades, we had the security organs, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me now what the relationship was of these security organs in the lower units, vis a vis the security organs at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, the order was known. The security organs at the levels of brigades, battalions and lower were directly subordinated to the security chiefs in the corps, and the chiefs of security in the corps were directly subordinated to the Security Administration, along the professional line. Otherwise, the security organs reported for their work to the commanders of their units. At the Main Staff level to the chief of staff at the corps level to the corps commander, at the brigade level to the brigade commanders. Only in the professional sense, when they performed counter-intelligence assignments, the superior officers guided the security organs at the level of the Main Staff, the corps, down to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In view of your answers and how you moved in the service, we can see that even before the war, you worked in the security organ, so I assume that you are familiar with the pre-war organisation of these bodies. So can you please explain, what does it mean that they were subordinated along the professional line?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: It means that in counter-intelligence work, the organs performing such assignments received instructions and were trained to go to their superior security officer. But in order to execute the complete assignments, the unit commander knew about this, whether it was a brigade, corps, the Main Staff, and so on and so forth. So purely professional assignments, in terms of how to actually carry out that task. The security organs were, in this sense, guided by the superior security organs, but as a whole all the security organs as well as other command organs were subordinated to the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pereula, how long were you at the Main Staff security organ?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I said that I was there until November 1993, when I was transferred to the Defence Ministry, where the Defence Minister issued an order to appoint me as the security organ at Pale. The minister at the time was General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe your duties that you were carrying out at the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: When I came to the Defence Ministry, my first assignment was to organise the security service at the defence ministries. Since these ministries did not have the adequate personnel -- security personnel. The security organs were at the level of the Defence ministry. Then we had the local or district ministries, and then the local ministry Defence sectors, such as Banja Luka and some other places. At the same time, I worked on their professional training and counter-intelligence protection of members of the Defence Ministry. Also, the Defence Ministry was in charge of wartime industries at the time, so it was also my job to provide security for these facilities. And of course we also had security organs located in some of these industrial facilities, in the factories such as Orao and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, I'm going to ask you to wait before you give your answer in order for everything to proceed smoothly. You told us what your duties at the Ministry were. Can you please tell us if there was any cooperation between the Ministry and the Main Staff and the security organs? And if so, at which levels did this cooperation proceed?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Cooperation between the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff functioned in all segments, including the security service. However, the security organs of the Defence Ministry were autonomous in relation to the security organs of the Main Staff of the VRS. But when we're talking about exchange of information, operative information, there was mutual cooperation. At the time, the Defence Ministry, among other things, had as its main assignment and the security of the army of Republika Srpska, and in that sense the security organs played their role, their particular role, especially if we keep in mind the wartime industries, the defence industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to your previous answer, when you spoke about those defence industry plants. You said that you cooperated with the security organs deployed in those defence industry plants. What plants are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, the defence industry plants were primarily Pretis in Vogosca, Orao in Rajlovac, the repair and maintenance facility in Hadzici. There was a plant in Doboj and Kosmos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the Ministry and those plants ? Did they have any contacts at all?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, the cooperation of security organs at the level of the Defence ministries and the security organs in the Republika Srpska army was at the highest level when it came to defence industry, because in the areas of responsibility of the units where those plants were located, the JNA security organs that obtained some intelligence, this is where operational exchange of information was carried out, at the level of the Defence Ministry and the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether, in this period while you were at the Defence Ministry, did you have direct cooperation with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. I worked with him to the extent that was necessary to exchange operational information and intelligence obtained by the security service in the Ministry of Defence and the security service at the Main Staff, because security organs in the units of the VRS were not duty-bound to provide information directly to the Ministry of Defence. What they did was they forwarded this information up the chain of command to the Main Staff, and then at the level of the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff, this information was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pereula, we are now going to deal with another topic. Did you have any knowledge -- were you involved at all in anything that had to do with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to say. While I was at the Main Staff, because there was a lack of security organs because the Main Staff -- the staffing level at the Main Staff was maybe 20 to 30 per cent of establishment levels, this is why I was involved in questioning prisoners of war. So in 1992, sometime in May, in Han Pijesak, I interrogated Mr. Meho Agic, the commander of the Rogatica Brigade. He had been captured at Bragolamin [phoen] by the VRS troops. This interrogation took place in the Han Pijesak police station, in the office of the police commander. And this man was questioned about the developments, in terms of war, the strength, goals, and objectives of this unit. After the interview, Mr. Meho Agic remained in the police station in Han Pijesak for maybe two days or so, and then he was transferred to Kula, to the prison there. It's in Eastern Sarajevo. And he was later on exchanged, and nowadays he lives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But do tell me, later on in 1995 until the end of the war, were you involved in the work of the joint commission that was set up to interrogate prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. In May, the Republika Srpska government convened a meeting that was chaired by the judicial organs, and this meeting was attended by the security organs from the Republika Srpska army, from the MUP. And the objective was to make a decision tasking all the units with gathering information about crimes against humanity and against international law, and submitting them to the judiciary. And in line with this, after the army of Republika Srpska entered Zepa, I was involved in the work of a commission that was supposed to interrogate the prisoners of war from the BH Army, the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I will have to interrupt you. We don't want to rush this. Who set up this commission to interrogate prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. But at the level of the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff, an agreement was reached to set up this commission, and the Ministry of Defence received a request to -- because there were not enough security organs in the Main Staff, to second one of the security organs to that commission. And Mr. Milan Ninkovic, he was the minister at the time, he approved my involvement in this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, who were the other people on the commission?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, I was there on behalf of the Ministry of Defence. There was a representative of the Republika Srpska Army, I think it was Lieutenant Maksimovic, representatives of the Interior Ministry. I remember it was Vojnovic, whose first name I can't recall, and there was another man from the MUP, again whose name I can't recall, but you can get this information from the orders. There was a representative of the Public Prosecutors' Office, Mr. Borovcanin, and a representative of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I asked who was there on the commission, I asked a general question, a representation of what organs, but thank you for the details that you've given us. When did this commission start working? What was its objective? Could you please clarify this a little for all of us, how this commission operated?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, on the orders of the Defence Minister, I became a member of this commission. And since I was the ranking officer there and I had experience in the security service, I was designated as the coordinator of the commission. We went to Foca, and we were headquartered in this hotel in Foca, Zelengora or whatever its name is. But at any rate, what really matters is that we were in the hotel. And in the prison, we were given premises from the warden to actually do our job, in operational terms; in other words, to interrogate those prisoners of war. There were 30 to 40 of them, if I can recall this correctly, and we organised a meeting. We did the work plan. There were four -- or, rather, three operatives who actually did that, and I was the coordinator. I interrogated two of the prisoners at that meeting, the first meeting. I relayed the instructions and the orders of Mr. Ljubisa Beara, who drew our attention to the fact that when working with prisoners of war, we should comply with the Rules of Service of the Security Service, the Law on the Army and international conventions. And once this plan was in place, we actually started doing our job. The operational tasks I can't remember now, but it was about seven days. It took us about seven days or thereabouts. After the prisoners were interrogated --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will ask you not to go so fast. We have already been warned that your answers must be responsive, so that's what I'm asking you now, to be responsive in your answers. Let us backtrack a little bit. Were judicial organs represented there? Did they provide any instructions about how this was to proceed, the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: The representatives of the Public Prosecutors' Office and from the Court were present there. I already indicated that Mr. Borovcanin was there, representing the Prosecutors' Office, and I think there was a Mr. Supic there, but I can't really confirm that, representing the Courts, and they participated in our work there. They assisted us when we did the summary reports based on the interrogation, indicating what elements -- what acts might constitute crimes, criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did this interrogation last?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I've already indicated the interrogations lasted for seven days. I'm sure about that, but -- perhaps longer, but I can't really tell you that. You can check that in the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who were those prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Those were prisoners of war, BH Army troops, the Zepa Brigade. That's what I'm calling it now. I think it had a different designation, whether it was the 1st Brigade, the 1st Drina Brigade. But at any rate, those were members of the Zepa Brigade. And in the course of the interrogations, I already indicated that I interrogated two of those prisoners, well, it's been a long time so I only remember that one that I interrogated was blonde, aged about 25, short, and in his statement he said -- well, it was our objective to determine, although we did have some operational intelligence from before, that until Zepa was demilitarised, this unit had perpetrated crimes against the civilian population and prisoners of war from the ranks of the Republika Srpska army in the border areas of the Zepa municipality, such as the village of Borovine and other locations, and it was our basic objective in interrogation of those prisoners of war to determine who actually did that or to confirm what we already knew, so as regards the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please, what specifically did you do once you did the analysis, you carried out the interrogations? You said that you did this analysis?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us a summary of the most salient points from the point of view of the security organs that you had the intention of learning or that you actually learned. So what were those prisoners, who were they, where they had come from, how were they captured, and what you learned from the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. After the interrogations were completed, we had a meeting where we did the summary report, and on the basis of this summary report, we drafted the criminal report. And this criminal report was then handed in to the Prosecutors' Office. But what you just asked me about, the objectives that we had and the facts that we ascertained, as I've already indicated, our goal was to determine what members of the Zepa Brigade of the BH Army had committed crimes in those border areas of the Zepa municipality, such as the village of Borovine, the murder of civilians, the members of the Borovine family, and the capturing of the Republika Srpska army soldiers, for instance an officer by the name of Milosevic, and we had indications that he had been wounded at the Batura mountain and that he had been captured, and he's still missing. His remains have never been found, and his family doesn't know about his fate. So in the course of the interrogations that I did, this prisoner of war stated that before the VRS entered Zepa, this brigade had set up some groups that were tasked with carrying out terrorist acts, attacking the Republika Srpska army facilities. There was a sabotage company in the Zepa Brigade, and it was tasked with carrying out sabotage action against Han Kran. And this man was part of this unit, their commander was wounded and -- in that action. Once the action was completed they returned to Zepa. In the meantime, the VRS entered Srebrenica, and the whole brigade, together with the command, it was at Travna Planina [phoen] near Zepa. I'm not sure about the location, but I think it's Travna Planina. They held a meeting to determine what they should do. So the entire Command, that's what this prisoner of war told me, participated in this meeting. The whole brigade was there, and they had a number of proposals and one of the proposals was to fight the VRS. Another proposal was to try to break through the areas between the units of the VRS towards Tuzla. And the third proposal was to do a forced crossing of the Drina river into Serbia. And the fourth proposal, that was the group that was captured, about 30 or 40 of them to move towards Rudo and to cross into Serbia there. The chief of the Zepa Brigade, Ramo Cardakovic, he was in a wheelchair, he was disabled, he proposed, in accordance to what this witness told me, that they should do a forced crossing of the Drina River into Serbia. Most of the troops in the brigade accepted this proposal. This is what this prisoner of war told me. And he didn't know what happened later, but he knew that his group managed to cross the Drina, and then somewhere near Rudo in Republika Srpska, they were captured by Republika Srpska troops and were brought to the penitentiary and correctional facility, the prison in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What you've just told us, this is your information that you reached by interrogating this prisoner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please, what was the period in which he said all of these things that you just referred to now?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Actually, he was talking about the period starting from June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And when were they captured?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but they were captured after a few days after the VRS entered Zepa. They managed to cross the Drina and to move towards Rudo. And that's where the units of the VRS -- I cannot remember the exact place that he mentioned. Probably it's there in the documents, exactly how they were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Any explanations provided by this prisoner about the way they tried to get out, was that before the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the fall of Zepa, because this group, headed by the brigade commander, were in favour of resisting by -- with weapons the army of Republika Srpska, and the one that tried to cross into Zepa was led by the police station commander. I can't remember his name. He's from Han Pijesak, and then he moved to Zepa, and he was the commander of the police station in Zepa. All of this was before the army of Republika Srpska entered Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to this main idea. You acquired information about the fact that crimes were carried out, and their perpetrators. Which event is this specifically relate to?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, specifically, let's start in order. A young soldier of the JNA who was captured in the beginning by the Zepa forces was mistreated and led through Zepa with the words "Here we captured a Chetnik." The name is -- no, I can't remember the name exactly, but it's written there exactly which member of the B&H Army did this, and it's true this soldier was later exchanged and returned to the JNA. This is one thing. Another thing, we got information about which persons burned the village of Borovine and committed a crime there against the civilian population. It's been a long time since then, I cannot recall all the names, but it's documented. It was also confirmed that Officer Milosevic was wounded in a personnel carrier and that he was captured in such a state, and this prisoner knows who was the commander of which section and he mentioned that. However, he doesn't know then what happened with this officer of ours later. So, as I said, his body has not been found to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then you obtained information that the perpetrators were actually suspected to be in the prison in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. By questioning and making a summary report, and by citing in the criminal charges, we included a small number of people from that group that was in the Foca penitentiary. But according to what they said, the bulk of those B&H members of the Zepa Brigade crossed into Serbia with their chief, Ramo Cardakovic, and we were unable to get to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the end of this whole procedure, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I said that. At the end of the procedure, we conducted an analysis, we drafted a report, we put together a charge sheet, and we passed that on to the Prosecutors' Office. As for what the Prosecutors' Office did after that, I personally don't know. This was not part of the security organ's job. But according to some information, these prisoners that we interrogated in the Foca penitentiary were -- they stayed in prison after we left, but later I got some information that all of those persons were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pereula. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have completed this part of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I indicated that I will have no cross-examination, but in order to avoid any misunderstanding, because there was some mention of the name Borovcanin, can I just be allowed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, because although he was mentioned as coming from a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, I'm Aleksandar Lazarevic, and I represent Ljubomir Borovcanin with my colleagues before this Tribunal. Unfortunately, he's not here today, he's sick, but I would like on his behalf to put a couple of questions to you. In order we can clarify, since you mentioned the last name Borovcanin during your testimony and you also did not mention the name?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall the name of this gentleman, Mr. Borovcanin, that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I cannot recall the name exactly, but I can describe him. He was short build with dark hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help you, in a way. Can we put on the e-court 2D 526. This is an exhibit that was used previously.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I know reliably that this person, Borovcanin, whose first name I cannot recall, worked in the Military Prosecutors' Office of the Main Staff of the VRS, and that is that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when you talked about the Prosecution and the Court, you were thinking about the military court?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, the bodies involved here were the Military Court and the Military Prosecutors' Office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise since we overlapped, your answer and my question. What I did was suggest to you in this document, what it says is that -- it says that: "President of the Court, Luka Borovcanin," in the military court and tribunal in Bijeljina. Is that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So what we establish is that we were talking about Luka Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madame Fauveau, you're still not cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic. You had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Pereula.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic, and I'm defending General Gvero and I'm going to put to you some questions to you in relation to your testimony today. You mentioned that you are from the Rogatica sector. Did you have any opportunity to go to Zepa during your duties in the area?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. I said that as a teacher, before the war, I worked in Zepa, and during the war, when Zepa was declared a demilitarised -- or, rather, a safe zone, I, representing the Main Staff, was part of a commission to monitor -- or at the time the UNPROFOR, the army of Republika Srpska, and the B&H Army reached a decision to form commissions representing the VRS, the B&H Army and the UNPROFOR to monitor the hand-over of weapons or, rather, to carry out the demilitarisation of that area. So in that sense, I went to Zepa to carry out these assignments, and our route was Sokolac, Rogatica, Borike, Sjeversko, Boksanica, Zepa. Well, this is actually my route, my old route that I used to take before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see when the check-points were set up of the UNPROFOR and the army of Republika Srpska? What I'm specifically interested in is if there were any check-points between Rogatica and Zepa on the road, on that section of the road.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: When Zepa was declared a safe zone, then -- well, there's 40 kilometres from Rogatica to Zepa. At the time, that section from Boksanica -- or better said from Sjeversko to Rogatica, was a free zone of Republika Srpska, where the population moved around freely and there was no need to set up any kind of check-point. There was a check-point at Boksanica which was set up by the Ukrainian Battalion, and it was an area of separation between the army of Republika Srpska and the B&H Army, regardless of the fact that Zepa was a safe zone. There was no check-point between Rogatica and Zepa, except Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in view of the configuration of the terrain, how much time do you need to drive from Rogatica to Zepa in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I said that the distance was some 40 kilometres. Before the war, it would take me at least an hour and a half by bus. Now I hear that the road has been repaired and asphalt has been placed from Brezova Ravan to Zepa, so it could be shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean after the war?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after the war, after the signing of the Dayton Accords, this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the end, you explained your duties at the Defence Ministry. Did you have an opportunity in your work to go to the Main Staff or to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. First of all, I said that there was cooperation between the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff, as a whole, and between certain organs such as the security service, which cooperated in the exchange of information with the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka, so that I would go to Crna Rijeka after I went to the Defence Ministry or, rather, Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, this is what I'm interested in, did you see General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, look. When General Gvero came to the Main Staff, we met at the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka, and it just happened that my son was in the traffic section and he would drive General Gvero. He was his driver until 1993, when he went to assume other duties, my son. So Mr. Gvero, General Gvero, and I knew each other very well. I would often go to Bijeljina, to the Ministry -- Defence Ministry section there, the Municipal Defence Ministry as well, and I had to go through Han Pijesak. So on my way back from Bijeljina, I would stay at a motel, Gora in Han Pijesak, where the logistics section was headed by the late General Djukic. And in 1995, in early May, I was returning from Bijeljina, and I dropped by at the hotel, and the chief of the traffic sector, Kerkes, said, "General Gvero is here, too. You can visit him," because he knew that we were like that, we were good friends. And I said, "Where is he?" And he said he was on the second floor of the hotel, and I went up there to see Mr. Gvero. We had some coffee and we had a kind of private chat. We said hello. And that's how I found out that Mr. Gvero -- that his office was transferred to the Gora Hotel in Han Pijesak, whereas before it was in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that period in 1995, did you visit General Gvero at this hotel?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, as I said, every time I went. I mean, there was no special visit. When I was travelling on official business, I would drop by. If I had any reason, then I would go and see him. And we would just drink coffee mostly, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, do you perhaps remember the car that your son was driving when he was driving General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I really don't remember the kind of vehicle, but the traffic people would know that, transportation people would know that, because they mostly allocated vehicles and drivers, who would be driving whom. So I'm not really able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pereula. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Sarapa, do you have any questions of this witness? You had requested ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, we don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Which brings us to you, Mr. Nicholls. Incidentally, I should have done this in the beginning of the sitting, but I had assumed you had been informed, too. The sitting schedule for today, up to and inclusive of Wednesday, will be from 9.00 to 10.40, so we've got another 10 minutes to go, and then we'll have a break, starting again at 11.10 up to 12.50, then a lunch break of one hour, and then resuming at 13.50 up to 3.30 in the afternoon. All right. So, Mr. Nicholls, do you wish to start now or do you wish to have -- I suggest you start and then we stop in ten minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My name is Julian Nicholls. I'm one of the prosecutors, and I'll be asking you questions. All right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, can you just tell me -- I hadn't known before now about your son driving General Gvero. How long did he do that for? When did he start driving him and when did he stop having that duty?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, upon General Gvero's arrival in the Main Staff in 1992, that's when it started, until November 1993, when my son, pursuant to the law that was in force at the time in Republika Srpska, he was granted leave to continue his studies. So he went to Novi Sad to continue his studies. So that was from 1992 until 1993. Until November, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after that, did he have that duty again later, to drive Mr. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, he never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. You described today the cooperation between the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff on important security matters. Well, I'm assuming these are one of the most important matters. Could you just describe what topics you should share information on? What were some of the more important types topics that you would coordinate with security of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: For the most part, this was operational information obtained through counter-intelligence work, and this information pertained, as I've already indicated -- the defence industry was located in the areas of responsibility of certain VRS units, and they had their organs in place, so they would obtain some operational information, operational intelligence, regarding the defence industry. So this was the information -- some of the information that I obtained from the Main Staff. The Ministry of Defence organs, when they obtained some information regarding the VRS, we would give this information to them. So this was done in professional terms. This was a professionally-speaking normal counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I understood you correctly, you went to the MOD in November 1993, was it?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where, physically, was your office in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: It was in the Ministry of Defence. That was in the Famos company premises, in their administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm sure it varied, but from 1993, November 1993, when you started there, through 1994 and into 1995, how often would you make that trip to Crna Rijeka or to Han Pijesak to meet with the Main Staff about security matters?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go there often. When it was necessary. When I obtained some information from my security organs, and if they were within the purview of the Main Staff and if it was necessary to have face-to-face discussions, then I would go, but otherwise this was also done orally by way of information. But when those were some subtle issues, I would go down there, but it was not that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the transcript says "subtle issues." Is that sensitive issues or things that needed to be done -- talked about face to face?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was counter-intelligence work that required some discussions and some arrangements to be put in place to do perhaps some work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you say "rarely or not often." I know it's a while ago, but can you just give me an idea? You know, once a month, once every two months, once a week, how often you had these face-to-face discussions with the Main Staff security?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, on the average, it might have been once every two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, other than these face-to-face meetings for the more sensitive issues, you said information was exchanged orally. How else would you exchange professionally information with the Main Staff during 1993, 1994, 1995? Is that over a radio, telephone, encrypted messages? I'd like you to describe the communication with the Main Staff, please.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, all communications went through the Command, through the headquarters, so the security service also used that route. But there were also written reports that were mailed, or, rather, couriers went around distributing mail. The security service did not have their own designated communications system that would go separately from the command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, thank you. If you can just keep talking me through this. When you get reports from the Main Staff, what happens with those reports? What did you -- you know, obviously you read them, but then what do you do with those reports?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: If the reports were of counter-intelligence nature, well, and reports in general, I would go through it until I obtained the information. All the information from -- that came from the Main Staff, I then informed the Defence Minister so he was kept abreast. The Minister also knew of the information that I was sending to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who was your immediate superior, the person you reported to? Was it directly to the Minister or was there anybody in between you and the Minister in the chain of that reporting?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, it was the Minister and myself. So I submitted those reports, and I told him about this intelligence directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let's take July 1995, June/July 1995. How often did you meet with the Minister of Defence and brief him on these reports?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I think that this period was the period when there was the least exchange of information between the Defence Ministry and the Main Staff, so I think that in June I did not receive any information from the Main Staff, and I did not relay this information to the Minister at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In July, when there was the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: The same. The Ministry of Defence was kept out of the loop as regards those events, except to the extent that other organs had to do it. But other than that, the security service did not have any need to get involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop here. We'll resume at 11.00 -- at 10 minutes past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just a few more questions on this topic about the cooperation and exchange of information between the MOD and the Main Staff. You say that June and July was the time of least information exchanged. The Ministry of Defence was kept out of the loop as regards these events. Why is that? Why, during these major operations, there's no exchange of security information?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: First, I am not aware if these were major pieces of information or not, but in any case the information that reached me from the field, from my subordinate security organs, did not indicate the need to pass this information to the Main Staff. I assume that something like that was also in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, that there was no need. I mean, I don't know what information was available to them, but there was no need to pass the information on to the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, just for -- a thought that occurs to me off the top of my head. There was this order in May to set up a commission to investigate war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you chaired and took a large part in that commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, no, we misunderstood each other. In May, I wasn't -- well, this was organised as part of the government, and the presiding role was played by the judicial organs, and this was in May. I wasn't chairing that commission. I was chairing the commission that was in charge of interrogating the prisoners of war in the Foca penitentiary in 1995, after the VRS entered Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly. So knowing that the VRS was going to enter Zepa, knowing that there would likely be prisoners to be interrogated, wouldn't you need some kind of information exchange at the time just to -- just to be ready and to know the situation on the ground for these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't know that the VRS would enter Zepa. This was not a part of my duties or within the ambit of the Defence Ministry. I didn't know that there would be arrests of prisoners of war. I mean, this happened after they entered. And before, I didn't have the information, I didn't know, and I did not take part in such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about Srebrenica; did you have advanced knowledge? Did the Ministry of Defence know about that in advance?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no. I had more contacts with Zepa, because as I said, when it was declared a safe zone, I was in a commission representing the army of Republika Srpska to effect the demilitarisation, and there was a different team that went to Srebrenica. So I'm really not that familiar with that side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And so you didn't go to Zepa in July 1995, yourself?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge of which check-points may have been set up, moved, during that time?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Before the VRS entered Zepa, I knew that because I had friends and relatives in Borike and specifically in Sjeversko, which is two kilometres away from the Boksanica check-point, I went to see Mr. Sretan Mitrovic, we were friends, and since I'm from Rogatica and I was in Rogatica in 1995, and even before 1995 the VRS entered, I went up there and I never saw check-points in that route. After the VRS entered Zepa, I didn't go along that route anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, going back to June/July 1995, can you tell us again the name of the Minister of Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Kovacevic's position at that time, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I don't know which Kovacevic you mean. There were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe his name was Momcilo, the one you referenced before.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I don't remember mentioning him in that context, but I do know Momcilo Kovacevic. He worked in the Defence Ministry on mobilisation and organisational issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that the -- and I don't want to go through this, the Court's seen it several times, even recently, but you are aware that the Main Staff sent a document to the Ministry of Defence during -- after the fall of Srebrenica, requesting that buses be mobilised and immediately sent to Bratunac. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't know that. That didn't go through the security service. And I responsibly state that I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So there were contacts between the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence that you were not aware of, if they were outside of security; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Perhaps, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at the order quickly to show you. 2899, please. And you know Petar Skrbic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here he's writing very urgently to the Ministry of Defence, requesting buses immediately, 50 buses, to be sent to the Bratunac sports stadium on 12 July; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states here, but I wasn't aware of that and I'm not aware of this order. And it was outside of my scope of duties, and it was probably the other department, whoever was acting from that department. That particular aspect was not part of my regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And then you're also not aware that Momcilo Kovacevic, that same day, responding to that order, sent an order for the immediate mobilisation of buses to go to Bratunac. That's 65 ter number 13. You're not aware of that either; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No. No, no, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What other departments would have been aware of that need to mobilise buses in order to move people from Srebrenica, in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot answer this. But, in any case, no sector or organ could have done that alone, if it was done, without the Defence Ministry, without the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's just, in that case, put this up to show you. Number 13, please. Can you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is that what you're talking about, this order -- this immediate, very urgent order, is signed "For," "Za," "Momcilo Kovacevic," and that would have gone through the Minister of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, as somebody who's been there since November 1993, at the top of the Security Department of the Ministry of Defence, why is it that you don't know what other departments would be involved in assisting in the Srebrenica operation, just as we've seen with these two documents? You have no knowledge of where the rest of the departments worked in your ministry?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Each department functioned separately and carried out its assignments with the consent of the Minister of Defence, so the Minister was aware of what each sector was doing, the sector for security, for mobilisation and organisation. I wasn't included in all of that. I didn't have to know all of these aspects, if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you learn that Srebrenica had fallen, or was liberated, depending on your terminology?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Simply, to tell you the truth, I actually learned about it through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I almost asked that as a leading question. You're another one of the high-ranking officials who learned about the fall of Srebrenica on TV or in the paper; is that -- you're sticking by that? You're in the Ministry of Defence, watching TV --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... okay. Now, let's go to the investigation of war crimes. You investigated war crimes against Serb civilians; correct? You told us about that.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I didn't investigate just war criminals who committed crimes against Serb civilians, but as part of the work in our town and the agreement at the level of the government, all crimes were investigated, regardless of whether they were committed by members of the army of Republika Srpska or of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This just exceptionally a case that I investigated involving members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995, when the army of Republika Srpska entered Zepa. This was an exception. Otherwise, the service's assignment was to investigate any person, including members of the army of Republika Srpska, suspected of committing crimes against humanity or committing violations of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And it's the duty, you know, of every officer in the VRS to report war crimes, crimes against humanity, crimes against civilians, that he becomes aware of; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you first start investigating war crimes committed by any party, regardless of the ethnicity of the victim, whether they were a Muslim, a Croat, or a Serb? When did you start this work?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I already mentioned the example, that I interrogated my first prisoner of war in Han Pijesak, Mr. Meho Agic, who was a member of the brigade. But as far as the Main Staff is concerned, I also dealt with personnel issues in the security organ and the issues of training, and if needed I was engaged on these particular tasks. And we have this Meho Agic, that's the example I referred to, who had been brought to Han Pijesak, and he was in the 1st Rogatica Brigade. Then we have also this instance that I described when it was agreed that I should be part of the team interrogating prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this Meho Agic, you knew him before the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the Staff of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Rogatica. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before the war started, you were on relatively good terms with him?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, speaking of war crimes, crimes against humanity, massacres of civilians, tell me about the most serious crimes committed by the VRS during the war that were investigated, that you know about. Let's just start with 1992. Who was prosecuted for killing Muslim civilians in 1992? You can't name one; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I cannot remember. And after all, when I was in the Main Staff, I was a desk officer, after all, and I was less involved in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I understand, but my point is you said that it wasn't just ABiH soldiers who were investigated, it was also VRS members, and I'd like to know if you remember --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- if you can point me to a single prosecution of a VRS soldier for committing crimes against Muslim civilians during the war period. Think about Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Zvornik, Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: As for Prijedor and that part of the Republika Srpska territory, since I'm not from that area, I didn't go much there and I'm not really that familiar with it, but otherwise I cannot give a specific answer to that question because I don't know. I'm not familiar with that. And when I said that we conducted investigations or that we were trying to find all the perpetrators of such crimes, this was the order from our superior officers. This is how I understood it, and this is how we were doing it. As for the fact that I didn't have a specific case, I said that I wasn't engaged on it that much. I was a member of the Defence Ministry, and the circumstances were -- or actually my duties were actually quite different compared to assignments like that. And in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You can finish your answer if you have something else to say. I didn't mean to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: The year 1992, up until 1993, was the beginning of the war. We were just in the process of being formed, so that it was impossible to find out things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about Visegrad; is there any prosecutions there for crimes committed by VRS soldiers, ever? If you don't know, say you don't know. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now -- and one of the things you talked about at length was this soldier, Milosevic, who'd gone missing and his body wasn't found. That was a priority for you, wasn't it, trying to get that information?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, it was a senior officer of the army of Republika Srpska, and we had reliable information that he was wounded and captured. However, we didn't manage to get information about what happened to the body. I think in the transcript of the interrogation of this witness or this prisoner, it's known what happened to him during the interrogation and what he said, but we don't know later what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And you agree with me, don't you, that it's a terrible thing for surviving family members not to know where the remains of their loved ones lie or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Absolutely, regardless of the side that is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me switch topics now a bit. You know General Miletic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you knew him in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
