utterances.text: And in June 1993, there was a Main Staff IKM in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was also at the HQ of the 1st Podrinje Brigade, Light Infantry Brigade, correct, in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I think that it was the forward command post of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But there's an IKM for the Main Staff in Rogatica, correct, in 1993, in June?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No. It was the forward command post of the Drina Corps, and some of the senior officers were then seconded to that command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll look at some documents about that in a minute. Now, the Brigade commander in Rogatica was Ratko Kusic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, Ratko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Security chief Zoran Carkic?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Miletic, in June 1993, was in Rogatica; correct? Some of the time, at least?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you communicated with him there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have 2742 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a VRS Main Staff combat order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pereula, the interpreters didn't catch what you just stated in reply to Mr. Nicholls' question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I was present at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, we'll get to it. I don't know if my friend had an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't know what he answered, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't actually an objection. The only thing is that we still haven't received a list of documents that the Prosecution intends to use. But I was informed by my assistant that we have just received it a moment ago, so that was it. I didn't have any objections at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Longer than a moment ago, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In any event, if you could look at this, sir, you can see that it's a 1st May 1993 VRS Main Staff combat order, and it's titled: "Combat Order for the Liberation of Zepa and Gorazde." Do you see that? Would you like a hard copy, sir, paper copy? Just let me know if you have trouble reading it. You can look at it as long as you want, but just let me know if you have trouble reading it.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, I can now peruse this the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the 1st of May, 1993, combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: The 1st of May, 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2 of the English and stay on page 1 of the B/C/S, we can see at the end of paragraph 1, as it states in the title, that this order concerns the Muslim enclaves, among others, in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, and it states that: "Considering the military defeats in Kamenica, Cerska and Konjevic Polje, and expecting the fall of Zepa within a short period of time," and it goes on to discuss the Muslim strategy. At the bottom of the next paragraph which begins: "Therefore ... ," the order states that the VRS needs to expect sabotage and terrorist attacks in the region of Grebka and the establishment of a corridor from Trnovo to Gorazde. Do you see all that? I'm just trying to put all this in context for you.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you were familiar with it. I'm just asking you if you can see that now, what this order was about.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to page 6 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, at point number 2 -- I don't think we have it there in B/C/S yet for the witness -- yes, point number 2, there we see the task: "The RS army has been tasked with the following: To mop up fully Sredoje, Gornje Podrinje." And then offensive actions: "To crush and destroy Muslim armed formations in the border area of Zepa and Gorazde, and to enable the Muslim civilian population to move out (transfer) to other territories, central part of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to recognise the rule of Republika Srpska and in that manner create conditions for the return of the Serbian population to the left and right bank of the Drina River." So that's -- so you see that, that's the task to be assigned?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to the next page of the English, page 7, which is page 5 of the B/C/S. We go down to the paragraph below the paragraph marked point 4. We can see that part -- the objective of the objection, one of the paragraph starts, is coordinated action on part of the Foca Tactical Group. And if we go to page 8 now in the English, which should be page 5 of the B/C/S as well, towards the bottom, we have: "The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska shall coordinate the operation from the IKM post in Rogatica. Colonel Dragan Ilic shall be responsible for merging, planning, linking, and RIK of the forces engaged in the liberation of Gorazde, and Colonel Radivoje Miletic of the forces engaged in the liberation of Zepa." And, finally, if we can go to the last page of both documents, at the bottom of the page, sir, you'll see that this combat order was drafted by Colonel Miletic. Do you see that.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: It says here the deputy commander, General Major Milovanovic. That's what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we need to go one page down. I'm sorry, page 9.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: On the left-hand side it says: "Drafted by."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now I want to go through a few documents, sir, following on from this, and see if it helps refresh your memory of what was going on at that time in 1993. The first one is 3565, and while we're waiting for it, I'll read out this document. Thank you. This document is from the 14th of June, 1993. It's from the forward command post. It says: "Main Staff, VRS, Rogatica. Extremely urgent." It's from Colonel Miletic. It's to be delivered to the Drina Corps IKM, I can't pronounce it properly, Cajnice, and it's for you to report to Rogatica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I really can't remember. But if that's what is written in here, then it must be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And there's -- there's nothing tricky here. I'm just trying to establish, as you can see, that there was this IKM in Rogatica, and Miletic was sending you a message at that time on the 14th. Can we go to 3566. And this is a couple of days earlier, the 12th of June, 1993. This is from you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's to the Tactical Group, Foca, intelligence officer, and at the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, Colonel Miletic personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as we can see, what you're doing here is reporting about one of the problems we saw in the combat order, is that the Muslim forces are trying to slip weapons into Gorazde, correct, which is something that would be of concern?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple more. 3568, please. We were at 12th June. We're back to 14th of June 1993. Again, it's from you to the Tactical Group, Foca, to the Podrinje Brigade in Rogatica and to Miletic. Take a moment to read this. And, again, here it's about Muslim units in this area are called "Grebka," which was also saw was a problem in the combat order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 3567, please. A similar document, 13th of June 1993. It's from you again at Drina Corps IKM, Cajnice, to the VRS Main Staff, to the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and again to Colonel Miletic. You can see that again; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again, this concerns the situation of the Muslim forces in Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's look at what you're proposing here: "Muslim forces in Gorazde have been placed in a very unfavorable position. Soldiers and citizens are in a state of panic. We decided to use our propaganda more in order to carry out further combat activities and realise our goal (liberation of Gorazde) as successfully as possible." And that goal is the same goal we saw in the combat order, correct, the liberation of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, this is subject to debate. There was combat, and the Serb forces before that had been defeated in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But it may be subject to debate, but it's not too complicated, is it ? The combat order we just looked at, and I don't want to bring it up again, is a combat order for the liberation of Gorazde, and you're saying that this proposal is to realise "our goal," the liberation of Gorazde, and that's one month later; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Well, that may be the terminology, the terminology may be to that effect, but there was combat, and let me repeat that before the army of Republika Srpska had been defeated in Gorazde, we can go over that, and then we mounted a counter-attack. This is where combat took place, and this is where I sent this information to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, about the liberation of Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What do you mean here --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: First of all, what I had in mind was to liberate the territory where we had been and from which we had been moved by the BiH forces, to be more precise, the Gorazde Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is part of, as it said in the combat order, allowing Serbs to return to the Podrinje region and have that region as theirs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's where we were, and we had been expelled from there, we had been moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, here is your suggestion: "To this end, we have composed a manifest which we intend to air on Radio Foca, Visegrad and Rudo, as well as on megaphone, which will be transmitted from a moving vehicle for greater efficiency. Please provide one armoured vehicle with a mounted megaphone from the direction of the 1st Romanija Brigade from which the following text will be broadcasted." So this is an element of propaganda in order to help you achieve your goal. This is the text that you suggested should be broadcast: "Muslims from Gorazde, you have realised that both the world and Alija have left you high and dry. Allah himself will help you if you listen to us. We offer you salvation, because we are the only ones who can save you. Break up from those who have driven you to death for months and take the road to salvation. Head towards Kopaci and Ustipraca. There we guarantee you life and final relief. There we offer you shelter and final deliverance and then a road of your choice. It is far away from the hell Alija took you to. Hoist the white flag and be on your way. We're waiting for you in Ustipraca. You don't have much time." Now, that is a message, I suggest to you, first of all -- wait for the question. First of all, it's directed to the Muslims of Gorazde, isn't it? That doesn't say "soldiers."

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Second, that message says "get out now." That message says "you don't have much time." That's basically a message any reasonable person reading it would think "leave or else"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No. When it comes to combat, in any case, everybody knows that propaganda is also used as a means towards a goal in combat. Some terms and expressions that are used here may be at the moment when they were used. In any case, one did not have in mind moving out the entire population of Gorazde, and I repeat that the environs of Gorazde at the time, the territory under the Serb forces, had been abandoned and we were given the task to return those territories. And when it comes to the terminology, obviously, when it comes to propaganda, you also used things that you didn't really have in mind as your goal. So I believe that this was just pure propaganda. We did not mention soldiers. This is an omission on our part. This is a -- something that could not be done in the situation of combat. You could not think of any single term, any single expression. This was just propaganda that was used as means in combat. Both sides did that. But it was not our goal to expel the civilian population from Gorazde, and indeed this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you read that message, a reasonable Muslim civilian in Gorazde would be frightened by that message and would hear, "There we guarantee, away from here, there we guarantee you life." That means Gorazde, "we're not going to guarantee your life." It says, "Hoist a white flag and be on your way." And it says: "You don't have much time." Now, for just a normal person in Gorazde, who's not in the military, isn't going to dissect this in a military manner, isn't going to say, Oh that's just propaganda. That's a threat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objections with regard to this issue. The Prosecution should first establish whether the message was read or not to the Muslim population in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm pursuing my cross-examination. This was a proposal made by the witness, that's where I am at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honours, I'm going there, I'm going to ask this question. I'm trying to do this in my own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, my colleague has essentially put the question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the response to Colonel Miletic from your proposal to broadcast this message to the Muslims of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I think that this message never reached the Muslim forces or the Muslim population in Gorazde, because we did not have the means to take that avenue. We could not air our message. We could not throw out leaflets from an aircraft or a helicopter. We did not have that. So I believe that this never reached Muslim forces. I believe that this was just something that we had prepared to do in order to possibly intimidate the fighters of the Gorazde units that were in their positions. And I personally believe -- I don't know whether you have at your disposal any document showing that the population of Gorazde never received this message in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, and I'm going to move on from this in a minute, but you certainly had control of the airwaves, the airwaves or radio stations, in Foca, Visegrad and Rudo; correct? There were radio stations that could broadcast there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I personally did not use them, and I am not aware of that. It may well be true, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may well be true because you suggested it in this proposal, and I take it that as a security officer, you don't suggest proposals that you know are impossible. You don't say, "I think we should do this," when in fact you know it's impossible. You don't say, "Let's use Foca radio station," when you can't use Foca radio station; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I really can't remember, as I sit here. It's very difficult for me to rewind and tell you how it all transpired. But I believe that at the time, these means did not function so as to be able to convey all the information to the civilian population in this particular way, to the Muslim population in Gorazde, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, it was beyond the means of the Main Staff of the VRS to provide one armoured combat vehicle with a megaphone on it; that was something that couldn't be done?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: We did not have that at our disposal, or at least I don't know that we had it at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving on to another topic. You talked about interviewing Meho or Mehmed Hajric at the SUP in Han Pijesak in 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You admitted to me earlier that you'd known him in Rogatica before this unfortunate war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, when you interviewed him, that when he was brought to you, that he had a head wound?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall, when he was brought to you, that he complained to you -- you interviewed him twice. I should say that.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, he just wanted me to find him a blanket and give it to him, because he was cold in the cellar. When he was first brought to Han Pijesak, I was not the one who established the initial contact with him. It was probably the MUP. I only saw him later on. He never complained of any wounds on his body, nor did I notice any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Because that's interesting, because what he says is that he complained -- that he asked for a blanket, just as you said, and also that he complained about being beaten to you; not that you beat him. You treated him fine, but he complained to you that he was beaten in between his interrogations with you. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No. Even eyeball-to-eyeball with Meho, I could tell him that he never complained about that to me. He was thirsty, I gave him water. I offered him cigarettes. Not mine, mind you, they were his own cigarettes that I located somewhere and I offered them to him. But he never complained about being beaten, and I never noticed anything on his body, although we spent a rather lengthy time talking, maybe an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember ever, you know, hearing about prisoners being beaten when they were in VRS custody?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. And if you would, you would have reported it, wouldn't you, and there would have been a prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I would have condemned that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you're from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There was a prison where prisoners of war were kept in Rogatica in July 1995; right? Are you telling me you don't know about Rasadnik? Let me help you remember, I might have pronounced it wrong. You have heard about it? We didn't get your answer.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Rasadnik, you're saying? Rasadnik? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There was a farm there that was used as a prison in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You're from Rogatica. You were a security officer. You're at the top of the MOD. You know about check-points from going home and talking to your neighbours and friends. Is it possible or was there a prison farm in Rogatica in July 1995, or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: There was a prison. I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever interview prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there were prisoners from Zepa held there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: This was not in my jurisdiction, and I did not get information about that from the superior command and I did not interrogate such prisoners in Rogatica. These prisoners were probably previously captured from Zepa or other places when I was -- while I was at the Ministry of Defence, so this was not part of my duties. There was no need for me to interrogate those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just give you a little background. These prisoners from Zepa, some of them, many of them, were men from Zepa, Muslims, who'd been removed from buses during the convoy removing them from Kladanj in July 1995. Now, you're interviewing prisoners in Foca to get information about war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In Foca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Prisoners are being interviewed in Rogatica about Zepa and about war crimes and about intelligence. Isn't it important to put that information together? Don't you need to know what's going on, what these prisoners are saying, if you're going to interview your prisoners effectively?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: First of all, I wasn't the person working on the coordination of these prisoners. Upon request of the Main Staff, I would go to Foca. There were no requests arriving at the Ministry of Defence to engage security organs on interrogations of prisoners in Zepa who happened to be in Rogatica, so I never went there and I never did any interrogations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you aware that prisoners, Muslim prisoners held in Rogatica, have reported being beaten? Did that ever reach your ears?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No. I must explain. I was born in Rogatica. In 1968, I came to Sarajevo, and I described my advancement in the service. I had no connections with Rogatica, other than having the TO duties, and it was my duty to visit the TO staff. So I was there officially during the war. I actually went to Rogatica very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I tell you that Muslims from Zepa held there, Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, men who were leaders in the community in Zepa, that they were beaten in that prison and then their bodies were found in mass graves, that's -- is this the first time you're hearing it, from me now?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I'm hearing it from you for the first time, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, about how many prisoners was it that were available to be interrogated in Foca? It might have been 149?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No, no, there were 30 to 40 prisoners in Foca which we interviewed. I don't remember if it was 30 or 40, but that was the figure, approximately. Over 100 persons are on the charge list, and these are mostly people who were in Serbia, who had crossed into Serbia with the chief, Cardakovic, and we couldn't get to them. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And these were members of the Zepa Brigade, and it was important to interview them to find out about crimes they had committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I don't know who you're thinking of. Which prisoners, the ones in Rogatica or the ones in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Foca. I'm talking about Foca now.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, they were prisoners, through which we were supposed to find out who committed the crimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's important to document --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: -- against members of the army of Republika Srpska and the civilian population, because these had occurred. Borovine -- Borovine were burned and people were killed, and it was necessary to find out who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, what about the 28th Division out of Srebrenica? They also -- also, you've heard about excursions out of the Srebrenica enclave and crimes being committed by the 28th Division; right?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I can say that I cannot say anything specific about Srebrenica. I was not present there in any capacity, not as a security person or a member of any commission, so that all of that is totally unfamiliar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Listen to the question carefully, if you can. I'm asking you if you'd heard, not if you were there, not if you took part in a commission, if you heard about the 28th Division committing crimes against Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: That, yes, yes. Kravica -- there would be other villages, too, around Bratunac, around Srebrenica. Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Serious crimes, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Serious crimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this commission is set up, and these investigations are set up in order to document/investigate these crimes. There's overwhelming evidence in this case about thousands and thousands of Muslim men, after the fall of Srebrenica, being held in schools all over Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that, not just -- I mean, have you ever heard that in the media, anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not aware of any commission set up to go to Zvornik and interview Muslim prisoners, are you, to see if they had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any of that, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what was your job, what were your duties, in 1997?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: In 1997, I was in Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, within the staff unit of the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, to secure the General Staff command post and the infrastructure in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And you worked as a personnel officer at army post 74 --

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't working as a security organ at the time, but I was working as a personnel officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From 1997 until the end of December 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And part of your job there had to do with paying VRS salaries; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: To pay salaries to members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you entered data as part of that job to make sure that salaries were paid to members of that VRS unit in Han Pijesak; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there was a salary differential in place then, where VRS officers got paid a differential if they were to make the pay commensurate to the JNA; correct? Some officers received a salary differential, and you were one of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Yes, correct, but I think that it was a little bit different. I think the salary was higher at the time in the army of Republika Srpska than in the JNA, so that was the differential that was paid to the senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said it better than I did. That's exactly right. And one of those serious officers that was getting paid there at the time you were there was Ratko Mladic; correct? He was on the list that you were processing?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Correct, but -- may I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: At the time in 1997 -- 1996-1997, we received lists, salary lists, from Banja Luka, and we entered data for it. And General Mladic was on the lists, but at the time there was no document, either from the International Community or from any organ of Republika Srpska, to stop paying salaries to any officer, including General Ratko Mladic, and this is why the salaries were paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you knew he was an indicted fugitive at that point, didn't you, or is that something new you're learning today for the first time, that Ratko Mladic has an indictment against him from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I found out later that there was an indictment at the time. From what I know, General Mladic was not in hiding. He lived legally in Belgrade, in his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when you were there from 1997 to 2000, you didn't know he was indicted, when he was getting these payments?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: In 1997, no. Later, I didn't issue the payments, but I knew that there had been an indictment issued. But as I said, the principle of subordination is well known, and certain officers cannot decide on their own if they are going to pay a salary to someone and to someone else not. And I repeat again, at that time there was no documentation issued either from the International Community or the authorities of Republika Srpska government, and at that time, and I'm speaking about 1997, I was not in a position to decide about that on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions right now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a brief one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pereula, let's begin from this last item, the payment of salary to General Mladic. Can you please describe how this was done, and what was your role in this?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: I already explained that we were the General Staff staff unit, and our main assignment was to provide security for the post where the General Staff headquarters was. Then we received lists from Banja Luka to pay out salaries. We would just enter the workdays and what was necessary for the work list to enter. Once we filled that in, we would return these lists to Banja Luka, and that is how the salaries were paid out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we're talking about finding the perpetrators of crimes, including very serious crimes, did the security organs of the Main Staff primarily work on that, and which organs actually primarily worked on this?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: To discover crimes, well, according to the law, any senior officer that obtains information that a crime was committed is obliged to report this to the relevant authorities. And the security organs, as part of their duties, were supposed to investigate or find out if such crimes had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said the security organs. At which level?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Just repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From what level, from lower-ranking units or from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: You mean to find out if crimes had been committed? Well, all the organs had the task at the level from the lowest-ranking unit all the way to the top-ranking unit, but as I said, when uncovering such acts, and I cannot remember specifically, some time has passed since then, the security organs are instructed on the methods and the means of operation, and an organ could perhaps independently apply one method, perhaps an informative talk, but all the other methods had to be approved by the commander, and approval of the methods to be used would go from -- would be issued by the commander, and then from higher up, from the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about this procedure, where does this information go to, who is it handed over to?

utterances.speaker: SPIRO PEREULA
utterances.text: Once we got this information, this information would be passed on to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon, do you have any questions? Judge Stole? Mr. Pereula, we haven't got any further questions for you. Our staff will assist you and organise your return journey back home. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have any documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls? Mr. Lazarevic -- but Mr. Lazarevic asked a simple question on Borovcanin and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to tender. I believe it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I was taking it for granted that you didn't have any. Okay. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Sorry. Yes, Your Honours, some of the ones I used were already in, and I wanted to try to get that straight. So it would be 3565, 3567, 3568. I think that's it, Your Honours. And 66, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's it. Yes, of course they are admitted, and let's go to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we wait one second before we bring that witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am -- and I haven't had a chance to talk to my colleague about this, I apologise. But I am told there is an order that this next witness, Mr. Jovanovic, that he has been -- is a 92 ter witness, which we welcome. But I see a time estimate of 1.5 to 2 hours, so if we could just clarify that. We are hoping we have ten or fifteen minutes of -- as a normal 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's deal with this first. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that the Prosecution objected to 92 bis statements of these witnesses, then we can now hear them as 92 ter witnesses. We were not aware of that at first, when we planned this much time in order to hear the testimony of these witnesses. So, in any case, the examination-in-chief will really not take that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but how long will it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will need about 30 minutes for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's hard to say if this is a 92 ter witness, where a statement is going in, why 30 minutes is needed, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. In any case, there is something which is more important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, yes, Mr. McCloskey, I see you standing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't know if this is an old witness list -- exhibit list, but there's many, many exhibits on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, as we heard this morning, the Prosecution has, indeed, filed a motion, which is called: "Prosecution's Supplemental Motion to Require the Beara Defence Team to Adhere to Rule 65 ter, Rule 67(A)(ii), and the Trial Chamber's 27th May 2008 Order." We have discussed this preliminarily, of course, also taking into consideration the submissions that were made earlier by Mr. Gosnell, Mr. Nikolic, and Mr. McCloskey, and, Mr. Nikolic, we require a definitive reply from the Beara team, Defence team, by Wednesday - that's the day after tomorrow - depending of course on outcome of -- on the reply and the outcome of any discussions there might be between you and your colleagues and also the Prosecution, of course. We have -- we intend to hand down a decision by the end of the week. In the meantime, two witnesses are already at least in the pipeline, in relation to whom some concerns were raised, and our intention is to go along, but hear submissions as they may arise if any one of you encounters problems, and after hearing what you have to say, will take a decision separately on these two witnesses. So I'm saying, I'm limiting myself to these two witnesses, because we only heard some concerns being aired or being made in relation to them and not to others. If there are others, too, of course by the time and until we hand down our decision, we will act more or less in the same way. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As Mr. Nicholls had said, we are not making any -- we're ready to go with these witnesses this week. And what I had stated before about an exhibit list, I was looking at my exhibit list. We don't have an exhibit list from the Defence, so that may not be a problem at all. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic doesn't seem surprised. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't, not for these witnesses, no, we don't have any -- any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's bring in the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the next witness summoned by the Beara Defence team in this case. But before you start giving evidence, sir, you need to make a solemn declaration pursuant to our Rules, a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher, standing next to you, is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. Go ahead, read it, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nikolic will go first. He will then be followed, upon cross-examination, by others. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we start putting questions, I would like to introduce myself, although we did meet already. I'm Predrag Nikolic, representing Mr. Beara in his Defence team. Before you start replying and until you introduce yourself, a few useful pieces of advice so that this conversation of ours can be translated. It's necessary for you always to wait after I complete putting my question before beginning your answer so that the interpreters could translate that. Did we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you please now state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miladin Jovanovic. I was born on the 16th of October, 1952, in Bratunac, where I currently reside. I'm married. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about your educational background, and what about your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the School of Electrical Engineering in Tuzla, and I'm currently the chief of electrical distribution for the area of Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, where were you, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1992 and sometime the end of my [as interpreted] 1993, I was the general manager of the electrical distribution company in Bratunac, and after that, up until the end of the war, I was militarily engaged as a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to artillery, and I belonged to the Special Purposes Unit of rocket-launcher crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where was it deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This unit was deployed in the suburbs of Bratunac on the road towards Ljubovija in the construction material depot called Javar [phoen] Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you provided a statement to our investigator concerning the events surrounding combat activities around Srebrenica. Tell me, please, where were you around that time?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was in my military unit, and I've already told you that it was in the suburbs on the Bratunac-Ljubovija road. And on that particular day, I was scheduled to be on duty in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know Jovan [Realtime transcript read in error "Drago"] Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Jovan Nikolic. I had known him for a long time. He resided in the same town for a long time. He was a politician. He was the president of the Socialist Alliance, he was the principal of the school in Bratunac, and on that particular day he was the general manager of the farming cooperative in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, transcript, page 73, line 4, can we repeat the name of the person that the witness is currently testifying about in order to clarify the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Transcript 73, line 4, your answer is recorded as "Drago Nikolic." I asked you whether you knew Jovan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about Jovan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the eve of the events in Srebrenica that we're talking about, he was the general manager of the farming cooperative, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Around that time, did you have any communication with him, and what was the occasion if you did?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special happened around that time. We did not have any special contacts. The farming cooperative bordered on the premises where I was billeted together with my unit, and whenever I saw him, we would just exchange greetings, we would just exchange a few general comments, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Around that time, did he ask for any favours from you?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look, he was the general manager of the cooperative, and I've just told you that just an iron fence separated our two facilities, and on that evening when the incident in Kravica took place, Jovan Nikolic came to me and asked me whether I could take him to Kravica. That may have been around 2200 hours that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you take him to Kravica then?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said in my statement. I took Mr. Jovan Nikolic and two other men, Perica Vasovic and Mr. Eric, whose first name I can't remember at the moment, to Kravica that night. We stayed in Kravica between 15 and 20 minutes. I can't be sure of the time, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then Jovan Nikolic and the persons that you've just mentioned, Perica Vasovic and the third person, did they come to you together, asking you for a ride, or did you just pick them up on the way?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Jovan Nikolic came to ask me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we have a specific, special procedure when it comes to Rule 92 ter, and it is certainly not the one that you have chosen. Basically, you need to refer the witness to his written statement, the one that you would have circulated under that Rule, under 92 ter, which for all intents and purposes, basically, the examination-in-chief, and then ask him whether he attests that that written statement or evidence, that the transcript of that evidence, reflects accurately his declaration and what he would say if he were to be examined on the same issues and matters now. And then depending, of course, on his answer, you fill in any blanks that there are, you clarify any issues that may still remain undealt with in the statement, and there we are very flexible. We've been very flexible with the Prosecution, when it's been the case, and we have no intention of not being flexible -- equally flexible with you all, but we have to follow the procedure. In other words, you can't adopt a 92 ter procedure, and then pretending that that does not exist, and putting all the questions that you would have put to the witness if there had not been this either 92 bis or 92 ter. In the meantime, I'll give you time to organise yourself. It's time for a break, and I think it's an hour's break. Correct? It's an hour's break, and then we have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Nikolic, I suppose you got the message, so we should be able to conclude. And please do go straight to what is required by the third paragraph of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is exactly what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you provided a statement to our investigator, Milan Stanic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It says in the statement that it was in April 2007.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the statement, did you speak about your departure for Kravica? This is what we tackled just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this statement, you still have to ask him using -- I mean, doing it the way the Prosecution was instructed by us to go about it, whether the witness attests, or confirms, in other words, that the statement you just referred him to - if he needs to see it, we give it to him - accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if he were to be examined on exactly the same issues today. You need to clear that hurdle first, and then go to supplementing or clarifying anything that is necessary, but not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we have just heard that you signed the statement. If you were to speak about the same things today, would you say the same thing and would you sign them?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the statement and ask you to confirm whether the signature on the statement is indeed yours. Could you please be so kind and provide the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The questions that you were asked in the statement, would you provide the same answers to them today?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the part that refers to your arrival in Kravica, would that be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And also the part that refers to the conversation that took place in your car on your return from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm faced with a dilemma here. This is not so much about the statement as it is about my true recollection, as it was at the time. Kravica, as a case, was a very difficult case. Those were the days that I would gladly erase from my memory, if I could. When it comes to the Kravica case, there are lots of rumours and stories going around in Bratunac at the time, starting with somebody saying that a soldier was strangled with bare hands by the detainees. There was also a story that he was killed from a rifle, another one according to which he had been run over. This all created a chaos in my head, and I sit here, I really can't remember what I heard at what specific period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Jovanovic. When I asked you whether you would adhere to your statement and whether you would provide the same answers about the conversations that you -- conversation that you had in your car, let me tell you that in your statement, you confirmed that you did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would still adhere to that as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we come to the conclusion of Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can I have the 65 ter number of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just bear with me for a moment, please. I apologise. I'm not sure about the number. Would I please be allowed to provide this to you a bit later? I don't want to make any mistakes that would need to be corrected later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It seems that my cross-examination will not last as long as I indicated. I mean, it's significantly reduced by the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic. Just for the record, my name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I represent Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin, together with my colleagues, Ms. Cmeric and Christopher Gosnell. We represent Mr. Borovcanin, and in his illness, on his behalf I would like to ask you a few questions that concern your statement and your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can, in the meantime, we have -- is it in the statement as it is in e-court already or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go ahead, and then we'll see if we need to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is my understanding that it is P3595 in the e-court. [Interpretation] I would like to call up document number P1536 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1356"] in e-court. This is a photo, an aerial photo. 1563 is the number. I apologise. There seems to be a mistake in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you recognise the facility that you see in this aerial photo?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the farming cooperative in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now I would like to ask the assistance of the usher. I would like to have the witness mark certain things in the photo. As it is, you draw the pen across the screen, you will make a mark, just to let you know how it's done. First of all, could you please place an arrow by the road, and put a letter "B" next to it to denote the direction that you have to take to go to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if I understood your testimony correctly, and if I understood the statement you provided to the Beara team correctly, together with the other persons whom you have mentioned, you took a car, in the evening in Bratunac, and you arrived in the farming cooperative in Kravica. Could you please mark, in this photo, the direction from which you came and the route that you took in order to get there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the record, let us just say that the dotted line represents the road that the witness took together with the others to arrive at his destination. If we look at this aerial photo and your markings on it, we can see that on the way from Bratunac, you turned left and then right, and that is where the entrance into the farming compound at Kravica is located; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: If you take a car and if you want to enter the compound of the Kravica farming cooperative, is this the only way to do it? Is there some other side gate through which you can take your car in?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's no such thing. This is the only way you can enter the compound by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Around the entire compound, there is a fence, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is an iron fence which fences the compound off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now put your initials and today's date in the right lower corner of this photo?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] What is the date today, please? 28th. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And now I would like to display the document again, another clean copy of document number 1563 without the witness's markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here, you have the same photo again, and I would like to ask you to mark the place where the car stopped on that night, on the 13th. Could you please give us the exact position of the place where your car stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have just one question. Do you want me to mark the place that I reached or where I left the car when I returned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Both. First, can you mark the place where you stopped the car?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then it would be number 1 [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then there is also a place number 2 [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In order for us to be able to understand what you're talking about, let us put it this way: First you stopped at location number 1. Then you made a U-turn or you turned around within the compound, and you returned to place number 2, and this is where you parked your car; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you also put your initials and today's date in the bottom right corner.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you arrived -- this document can be saved, but I would like the witness to be able to see it still. At the moment when you arrived at the place that you marked "1," according to your testimony or, rather, according to your statement, you heard an order for all -- for the lights to be turned down?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The order was, "Turn off your light and go back."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you complied with the order. You turned around in your car. Then you returned to place number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your passengers who were in the car on that evening, Eric, Jovo Nikolic and Perica Vasovic, where did they leave the car? Did they leave the car in place number 1 or place number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In place number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This means that they got out of the car, you double-parked, then you heard the order for lights to be dimmed and for you to return --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's when I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this explains quite a bit of things. And let me now ask you this: When you were there, did Jovo Nikolic carry anything in his hands? Did he have anything in his hands?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. As far as I can remember, he didn't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And while you were sitting in the car, although the photo illustrates that pretty well, you could not see what the three of them were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not see that. There was no line of vision, first of all. And, second of all, it was already night. It must have been around 10.00, half past 10.00 in the evening by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you something else. Did you get out of the car at all or did you remain sitting in the car?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not get out of the car at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were sitting in the car, did you hear a loud argument, a quarrel? Could you maybe discern the voices of Jovan Nikolic of -- or any other of your passengers or somebody else? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard some swear words, which I cannot repeat because I can't remember, but I remember that there was some swearing going on. But I did not understand everything well. I don't know, there must have been also an element of fear present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you remain sitting in your car before your passengers returned?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe some 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the three of them get to the car?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you get out of the car at all when you see them approaching, or did you remain sitting and they got into the car?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They just got in. I never left the car, never got out, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the car, waiting for your passengers, did you hear any shots, any shots fired?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear shots coming from various directions. It was night, so it was very hard for me to tell where those shots came from. It's pretty much enclosed with the hills. There was a lot of echo, so it's not very easy for me to tell where the shots came from. My feeling was that there were shots coming from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us precisely whether the shots came from the hills, from the direction of the hangar, or from east or south?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. It was night, it was very quiet, so the hills were resounding and it was impossible to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us whether those shots came from various directions or just from one direction?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My opinion is that they came from all over the place, from different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like us to deal with just one more issue. You gave the statement, but let us clarify this. Did you see any persons in uniform or any other persons within the compounds of the Kravica farming co-op?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see anyone, except for this shadow of this man who ordered me to turn my car back and to go back where I came from, and I didn't see anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "shadow," a silhouette, does that mean that you cannot tell -- that you cannot tell us any details about what kind of clothes that person was wearing, what age that person was?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I told you it was at night, it was at 2200 hours, 2230, it was dark. And also I was a driver. I was there to operate the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today, in answer to questions asked by Mr. Nikolic, who also examined you, you said that from July 1995 until now, there have been many stories, rumours, about what had happened, how it had happened, and I assume that even today this is a topic that crops up in conversation among the people there in Bratunac. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those ten days or so, that was the burning issue in the town, the key topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And even after those events, people talked about it, and they indeed talk about it today?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people talk about it to this day, because it was a specific day, a key day that remained in the memories of the people there, and nobody can forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you've already told us, those stories are different stories?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what people are like. When a story is recycled twice or three times, everybody embellishes on it. Details are added all the time. Everybody adds their own little thing. So there were various versions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you one more question. As far as I can recall, the first time that you gave your statement was in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that's ten years from the time of the events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this fact that we mentioned a little while ago, that there were so many different stories, that you heard different versions, and that people were talking about over this period of ten years, do you think that this fact may have influenced or, indeed, did influence your testimony, the statement that you gave, in which you detailed what you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those stories could not affect the key elements of the story, the essence of the story, but they did create this chaos in my brain, because I can no longer tell when I learned some of the -- some specific piece of information. Because of this deluge of information, I cannot tell you whether I heard something on the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 25th and so on, because this was talked about at the time and it is still talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. Maybe I should have raised this while still on my feet. But bearing in mind that we have just received this witness's testimony in the State Court in Bosnia, it was only an hour ago and we only received an audiotape and we didn't have time to listen to these tapes, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to reserve the right for some additional cross or something once my learned colleague finishes. Just that would allow us to familiarise ourselves with the content of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. What do you have to say to that, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it has come to you, Mr. McCloskey. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic. My name's Peter McCloskey. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor and I'll have a few questions for you. The first thing I want to do is if we can get up the 92 ter statement on -- I believe we're going to have to use the ELMO. It should be 3595, but I'm told it's not in e-court. And it's only in English, so if we could just put the first page of that on the ELMO. And, sir, I'm sorry that this is just for the English audience. I will -- if we could just put the first page up there, and if we could -- yeah, that should do it right there. I'll read slowly to you the section that I want to ask you about. It's basically the section where you get to the warehouse. You say: "The director of the cooperative at the time was Jovan Nikolic. He came to me that evening and asked me to give him a ride to the Kravica cooperative, which was an extension of the Bratunac cooperative. Jovan had information that something strange was happening at the Kravica cooperative. I took him to Kravica. With us in the car were Perica Vasovic and the late Miso Eric. I drove up to the cooperative compound. They exited from the car. I turned around and parked the vehicle behind the building in the compound. I remained in the car and did not go out. About 15 minutes later, Jovan, Perica, and Miso returned to the car, and we all went back to Bratunac. While waiting in the car, I heard gunshots coming from everywhere. When they came back to the car, Jovan, Perica and Miso did not make any particular comments. We were all frightened by that frequent gunfire and sought to get away as soon as possible." Okay. Does that remind you of the statement that you were asked about by Mr. Nikolic that you agreed to?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to take you to another statement you made. This is 65 ter 3592, and let me give you a Serbian copy of that report, because it's a report dated 21 September 2005 from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Security, State Investigation and Protection Agency, War Crimes Investigations Centre. Can we give that to you? I've made some blue marks on it just to show you the part I'm going to ask you about. Perhaps counsel wants to see where I made some marks. The top mark was a mistake. Ignore that one. The underlines was the ones I'm meaning to talk about. So, sir, do you recall giving a statement in Bosnia to the State War Crimes Investigators back on 21 September 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to page 5 of that statement in the English. It's page 3 in the B/C/S, but the witness has the page in front of him, and I underlined the section where you get to the warehouse and I want to read that out to you now and ask you some questions. Basically, in the middle of the page in the English, and it's about two-thirds of the way down the page in the Serbian, you say: "I remained in the vehicle while my three passengers went to the administrative building of the cooperative, which is on the right-hand side from the entrance to the premises. While I was sitting in the vehicle, I heard bursts of gunfire and individual shots from infantry weapons coming from everywhere, and from the direction of the hangar, human screaming, cries and swearing could be heard. I found it quite gruesome. We stayed there for approximately half an hour, when Djole and Perica got into the vehicle, and then we returned together to Bratunac, where I dropped off Djole and Perica in front of the residential building Lamela, where Djole lived then and where he lives today. "I returned to my regular activities in the unit, that is to say, to my duty. I cannot recall whether Miso Eric came back with us. I learnt, from the conversation in the car that night on our way back to Kravica from Djole, that a group of captured Muslims from the area of Srebrenica was in the hangar. He did not say how many were there, but he did say that this group was guarded by special police from Skelani and that they had problems guarding them because they were not kept in an enclosed area. Djole also said that one of the members of the special unit was strangled by Muslim prisoners that day and that members of the special unit were asking their command to send a rotation of troops or reinforcement because they were too exhausted to endure it physically." Do you stand by the information in that statement to the BiH that I just read?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain a little while ago the discrepancy between the statement that was given in Sarajevo and the statement that I gave the last time, my last statement, and I say the same thing. I am no longer certain. I know that I had this information in my head, but I don't know -- I can't determine the timeline as to where and when I got specific pieces of information. The fact is that I do have this piece of information that a soldier was killed, and I have this piece of information that chaos ensued. I gave you various versions of it. They were different versions, how this unrest occurred and how this soldier was killed, but to this day, after all those statements, no matter how hard I try to actually remember, I can no longer be certain when, on what day, at what time, I actually heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question. My question was: Having looked at this statement that you gave in 2005, when this would have been fresher in your memory, do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've tried to explain to you that I cannot stand by that statement, because I am no longer certain whether I heard that on that night or at some other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked pretty much a very similar question by the State Court Prosecutor a few months ago, whether you stood by that statement? This was in a trial, the Kravica trial at the State Court.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that Kravica is something that is quite striking, something really gruesome. This is not something that you can forget. But the timeline, the chronology, please believe me when I say that I cannot say when I learnt of this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I just ask you if you remember testifying in Sarajevo in the State Court case.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that I remember that. I remember that I was in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: 2005. I don't know the exact date, but you can see it here. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about your testimony on the 4th of July, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's when I testified as a witness in Sarajevo, and that's when I provided the statement, but I am not sure whether at that time I was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. Do you know Ljubisa Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin worked in the Bratunac SUP before the war, and I personally knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in the Bratunac police station during the war, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not all the time, but for a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was he there during the famous Muslim attack on the village of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I was just a rank-and-file soldier, and I didn't know who was assigned where.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you who was assigned where. I just -- do you remember that Mr. Borovcanin was a police officer in Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
